text.tspan: Why a model needs to be told the order of the words

Attention, the heart of a Transformer, has no idea what order the words came in. It compares every word with every other word and takes a weighted average — and an average does not change if you shuffle what goes into it. So without help, "the dog sat on the floor" and "floor the on sat dog the" would look
" means exactly the same thing on both sides of the model.

text.tspan: A · The call stack, with the tensors at every step
Position is calculated, not learned — the frames show where

Positional encoding is easy to mistake for something the model learns. It is not: the six construction frames run before any data exists and never run again, and the six forward frames only read what they left behind. Keeping those two halves visibly apart is most of the explanation.

B · Why the table looks the way it does
Where the pattern of the sine/cosine table comes from

The formula looks arbitrary until you see what the columns actually do. The left-hand columns swing quickly and tell neighbouring positions apart; the right-hand columns barely move and say roughly where in a long text you are. Together they give every position a unique pattern.
The frequencies, from fastest to slowest

text.tspan: the left columns change quickly from row to row; the right columns hardly change at all — that is the whole design
What the model actually knows about order

Two facts worth remembering. First, this table is the same for both sentences and for every batch the model will ever process — it depends only on the position number, never on the words. Second, nothing later ever asks "what position is this?" again: after
the position is simply part of the
word order the same way it works out everything else — by comparing vectors.
